title: Gauss's Theorem: Flux, Divergence and Gauss's Law
short_intro: Gauss's theorem relates the total flux of a vector field through a closed surface to the total source enclosed by that surface. It simplifies the evaluation of electric and gravitational fields for systems possessing high symmetry.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of electric field using Gauss's law for infinite line charges, infinite plane sheets, and spherical shells, along with basic flux concepts.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Differential form of Gauss's theorem (divergence theorem), gravitational analogues, Gauss's law for dielectric media, and field energy calculations.

prerequisites: Solid angle subtended by a surface

concept_notes.heading: Statement of Gauss's Law in Electrostatics
bullets: The total electric flux through any closed hypothetical surface (Gaussian surface) is equal to 1/ε<sub>0</sub> times the net charge enclosed by the surface.
Only charges enclosed within the Gaussian surface contribute to the net flux; charges outside contribute zero net flux.
The Gaussian surface must be real or imaginary, continuous, and closed, chosen cleverly to exploit the symmetry of the charge distribution.

concept_notes.heading: Gravitational Analogue of Gauss's Law
bullets: The surface integral of gravitational field intensity over a closed surface equals -4πG times the total mass enclosed.
Expressed mathematically as ∫ g · dA = -4πGM<sub>enclosed</sub>, reflecting the attractive nature of gravitational forces.
Useful for calculating gravitational acceleration inside and outside solid spheres and spherical shells.

concept_notes.heading: Differential Form of Gauss's Law
bullets: Relates the divergence of the field directly to the local source density at any point in space.
For electrostatics, ∇ · E = ρ / ε<sub>0</sub>, where ρ is the volume charge density.
For gravitation, ∇ · g = -4πGρ<sub>m</sub>, where ρ<sub>m</sub> is the mass density.

concept_notes.heading: Symmetry Requirements for Application
bullets: Spherical symmetry allows the use of a concentric spherical Gaussian surface where the field magnitude E is constant and normal to the surface.
Cylindrical symmetry requires a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface for infinite lines or cylinders of charge.
Planar symmetry permits a pillbox Gaussian surface oriented perpendicular to an infinite sheet of charge.

derivations.title: Derivation of Gauss's Law from Coulomb's Law
steps: Consider a point charge q placed at the origin of a coordinate system.
The electric field at a distance r is given by Coulomb's law as E = (1 / 4πε<sub>0</sub>)(q / r<sup>2</sup>)r̂.
Calculate the electric flux through a concentric spherical surface of radius r: Φ<sub>E</sub> = ∫ E · dA.
Since E and dA are parallel everywhere on the sphere and E is constant in magnitude, Φ<sub>E</sub> = E × (4πr<sup>2</sup>).
Substitute E to obtain Φ<sub>E</sub> = (1 / 4πε<sub>0</sub>)(q / r<sup>2</sup>) × 4πr<sup>2</sup> = q / ε<sub>0</sub>.

derivations.title: Differential Form of Gauss's Law via Divergence Theorem
derivations.conditions: Continuous charge distribution and Gauss's divergence theorem
steps: Start with the integral form of Gauss's law: ∫<sub>S</sub> E · dA = Q<sub>enclosed</sub> / ε<sub>0</sub>.
Express the enclosed charge in terms of volume charge density ρ: Q<sub>enclosed</sub> = ∫<sub>V</sub> ρ dV.
Apply the divergence theorem to convert the surface integral into a volume integral: ∫<sub>S</sub> E · dA = ∫<sub>V</sub> (∇ · E) dV.
Equate the two volume integrals: ∫<sub>V</sub> (∇ · E) dV = ∫<sub>V</sub> (ρ / ε<sub>0</sub>) dV.
Since this holds for any arbitrary volume, the integrands must be equal pointwise.

formula_sheet.name: Integral Form of Electrostatic Gauss's Law
formula_sheet.variables: E = Electric field, dA = Area vector, Q_enclosed = Net enclosed charge, epsilon_0 = Permittivity of free space
formula_sheet.conditions: Any closed surface enclosing stationary charges

formula_sheet.name: Differential Form of Electrostatic Gauss's Law
formula_sheet.variables: \nabla cdot E = Divergence of electric field, \rho = Volume charge density, epsilon_0 = Permittivity
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid at every point in space where fields are differentiable

formula_sheet.name: Gauss's Law in Gravitation (Integral Form)
formula_sheet.equation_html: oint g cdot dA = -4pi G M_{enclosed}
formula_sheet.variables: g = Gravitational field, G = Universal gravitational constant, M_enclosed = Enclosed mass
formula_sheet.conditions: Closed surface in a gravitational field

formula_sheet.name: Gravitational Field of an Infinite Solid Cylinder
formula_sheet.equation_html: g = \frac{2 G lambda}{r} \text{ (for r geq R)}
formula_sheet.variables: lambda = Mass per unit length, r = Radial distance, R = Radius of cylinder
formula_sheet.conditions: Outside an infinitely long solid cylinder

formula_sheet.name: Electric Field due to Infinite Plane Sheet
formula_sheet.variables: sigma = Surface charge density, epsilon_0 = Permittivity
formula_sheet.conditions: Near an infinite, uniformly charged flat sheet

formula_sheet.name: Electric Field inside a Uniformly Charged Solid Sphere
formula_sheet.variables: q = Total charge, R = Radius of sphere, r = Distance from center (r < R)
formula_sheet.conditions: Internal points of a solid insulating sphere

formula_sheet.name: Electric Field due to Thin Spherical Shell (Outside)
formula_sheet.variables: q = Total charge on shell, r = Distance from center, R = Radius of shell

formula_sheet.name: Electric Field due to Thin Spherical Shell (Inside)
formula_sheet.conditions: For r < R (inside a hollow charged conductor or shell)

graphs_and_experiments.title: Electric Field vs. Distance for a Solid Insulating Sphere
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph with E on the y-axis and r on the x-axis. For r < R, a straight line passing through the origin (E proportional to r). For r > R, a hyperbolic decay curve (E proportional to 1/r²).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows continuous behavior at the boundary r = R, peaking at the surface and dropping off inversely with distance squared externally.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in multiple-choice questions regarding discontinuity or continuity of field magnitude at boundaries.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Electric Field vs. Distance for a Charged Conducting Shell
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph with E on the y-axis and r on the x-axis. E = 0 from r = 0 up to r = R. A sharp vertical discontinuity at r = R jumping to a maximum value, followed by an inverse-square decay for r > R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that the electric field inside a closed conductor is zero, with all excess charge residing on the outer surface.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via conceptual questions comparing insulating and conducting spherical distributions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Verification of Inverse Square Law conceptually via Flux
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Concentric spheres of radii r and 2r surrounding a point charge, showing identical total flux lines passing through both spherical areas.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Proves that total flux is independent of the size of the enclosing surface, depending only on enclosed charge.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to explain the solid angle approach and independence of surface geometry.

solved_numericals.question: A point charge of 8.85 μC is placed at the center of a cube of side 0.1 m. What is the total electric flux passing through the cube?
solution_steps: Identify the total charge enclosed: Q = 8.85 μC = 8.85 × 10<sup>-6</sup> C.
Recall Gauss's law: Total flux Φ = Q / ε<sub>0</sub>.
Use the value of ε<sub>0</sub> ≈ 8.854 × 10<sup>-12</sup> C<sup>2</sup>/(N m<sup>2</sup>).

solved_numericals.question: An infinite plane sheet of charge has a uniform surface charge density of 5.0 μC/m<sup>2</sup>. Calculate the electric field intensity at a point near the sheet.
solution_steps: Identify formula for electric field due to an infinite plane sheet: E = σ / (2ε<sub>0</sub>).

solved_numericals.question: A solid non-conducting sphere of radius R has a volume charge density that varies with distance r from the center as ρ(r) = ρ<sub>0</sub>(1 - r/R), for r ≤ R. Find the total charge of the sphere.
solution_steps: Set up the volume integral for total charge: Q = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>R</sup> ρ(r) (4πr<sup>2</sup>) dr.
Substitute the given density function: Q = 4πρ<sub>0</sub> ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>R</sup> (r<sup>2</sup> - r<sup>3</sup>/R) dr.
Evaluate the integral: [r<sup>3</sup>/3 - r<sup>4</sup>/(4R)] evaluated from 0 to R.
Result of integration: R<sup>3</sup>/3 - R<sup>3</sup>/4 = R<sup>3</sup>/12.

assumptions_and_limitations: Gauss's law is fundamentally a consequence of the inverse-square nature of forces (Coulomb's and Newton's laws); it fails for force fields that do not obey the inverse-square law.
While Gauss's law is always true for any closed surface, it is only useful for calculating fields when the physical system possesses high symmetry (spherical, cylindrical, or planar).

common_misconceptions.wrong: The term Q<sub>enclosed</sub> in Gauss's law includes charges located outside the Gaussian surface.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only charges inside the closed Gaussian surface determine the net flux through that surface.
common_misconceptions.why: External charges contribute equally to entering and exiting flux lines, resulting in zero net flux contribution.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The electric field E in Gauss's law ∫ E · dA = Q/ε<sub>0</sub> is produced only by the enclosed charges.
common_misconceptions.correct: The field E is the total electric field at the surface due to all charges, both inside and outside.
common_misconceptions.why: Although external charges cancel out in the surface integral, they still contribute to the local value of the total electric field vector.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Gauss's law is valid only for symmetric charge distributions.
common_misconceptions.correct: Gauss's law is universally valid for any distribution of charges, but analytical evaluation of E using it is only tractable under symmetry.
common_misconceptions.why: The law is a mathematical identity derived from Maxwell-Faraday equations; symmetry only makes the surface integral solvable.

quick_revision: Total electric flux through a closed surface depends solely on the net enclosed charge and is completely independent of the shape or size of the Gaussian surface.
Integral Form of Electrostatic Gauss's Law: oint E cdot dA = \frac{Q_{enclosed}}{epsilon_0}
Differential Form of Electrostatic Gauss's Law: \nabla cdot E = \frac{\rho}{epsilon_0}
